strapline: A K19.9 billion bill for the maize mountain, a rule-of-law ranking that stings, the President keeps his advisers — and Red Arrows take a one-goal lead to Durban

stories.title: The bill for the bumper harvest: Musokotwane asks Parliament for K19.9 billion more, three-quarters of it to pay farmers for maize the FRA did not plan to buy
stories.excerpt: Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane presented Supplementary Estimates No. 2 of 2026 to the National Assembly on Thursday 22 October. Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer report that K14.7 billion of the K19.9 billion is owed to farmers who sold maize to the Food Reserve Agency, which bought 2.7 million tonnes against a target of 500,000, and that K18 billion of the total is to be raised by borrowing on the domestic market.

image.label: Supplementary No. 2
image.caption: The second supplementary budget of 2026 is dominated by payments to farmers who sold maize to the Food Reserve Agency.

body: Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane went to the National Assembly on Thursday 22 October with a request for K19.9 billion in additional spending authority for the current year. Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer both report that the Supplementary Estimates of Expenditure No. 2 of 2026 were tabled under Article 203 of the Constitution, which provides for extra appropriations when the money Parliament has already voted proves insufficient. The 2026 budget was approved in December 2025; the Observer notes that a first supplementary budget for the year went through in April.

The bulk of the new money is explained by one decision. According to both reports, the Food Reserve Agency bought 2.7 million tonnes of maize in 2026 against an original target of 500,000 tonnes. The minister told the House that the Government chose to use this year's bumper harvest to fill the strategic reserve ahead of a 2027 lean season that he linked to El Niño. Zambia Monitor quotes him as saying that "the FRA purchased 2.7 million metric tonnes of maize just this year alone".

The Ministry of Agriculture takes K15.8 billion, or 79 per cent of the total. Of that, K14.7 billion is to pay farmers who delivered maize to the FRA this year, and K1.1 billion tops up the Farmer Input Support Programme for the 2026/2027 e-voucher season. The Ministry of Finance itself is allocated K1.3 billion, of which K1 billion remits 2026 Asycuda customs-processing fees to the Zambia Revenue Authority and K232 million brings additional World Bank grants onto the books for projects including the Catalysing Climate Risk Protection Shield for Zambian Smallholder Farmers, the Zambian Mineral Investments, Governance and Economic Sustainability project and the Irrigated and Sustainable Agriculture for Transformation project.

Education receives K540 million for the Higher Education Loans and Scholarship Board to cover shortfalls in tuition and student allowances this year; the Ministry of Defence gets K422.5 million for what the minister described as higher-than-expected operational costs of the security wings; and K300 million goes to the Contingency Vote for unforeseen spending in the rest of the financial year. Those itemised lines add up to roughly K18.4 billion; neither report sets out what the remaining K1.5 billion or so is for.

body.title: How it is to be paid for
items: K18 billion — additional borrowing on the domestic market, with details promised in a revised Annual Borrowing Plan
K1.3 billion — revenue collected above what was expected when the 2026 budget was approved
K510.8 million — additional funds from cooperating partners
K82.9 million — savings on external debt service
K27.3 million — unspent 2025 balances carried forward

body: Speaker Nelly Mutti referred the estimates to the Expanded Planning and Budgeting Committee, which is to report back to the House; the Observer says no date was given. The spending is subject to Parliament's approval. Neither outlet carried a reaction from opposition MPs or civil-society budget watchers on the day.

The request landed on the same day that the Ministry of Finance published the minister's account of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings held from 12 to 18 October. Zambia Monitor reports that Dr Musokotwane said the World Bank had committed to support Zambia's 2027 fiscal programme, that the delegation had met the IMF's African Department director Zeine Zeidane after a staff-level agreement on a proposed three-year Extended Credit Facility of about US$1.5 billion still awaiting IMF management and Executive Board approval, and that the Government's targets for 2031 include 10 million tonnes of maize a year, 10,000 megawatts of generation capacity, five million tourist arrivals and three million tonnes of copper.

body.text: Our priority for the next five years is growth, growth, growth.
body.attribution: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Minister of Finance and National Planning, in a ministry statement on the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, as reported by Zambia Monitor on Thursday 22 October

body.confirmed: That a K19.9 billion second supplementary budget was presented to the National Assembly on Thursday 22 October; the headline allocations and the financing plan, including K18 billion in domestic borrowing; the FRA purchase of 2.7 million tonnes against a 500,000-tonne target; and the referral to the Expanded Planning and Budgeting Committee — all reported by both Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer.
body.unverified: What the roughly K1.5 billion not itemised in either report covers; when the committee will report and when farmers will actually be paid; the terms and timing of the extra domestic borrowing, which await the revised Annual Borrowing Plan; and how the opposition and independent analysts will respond, since no reaction had been reported by Thursday evening.

GOVERNMENT PROPOSES K19.9 BILLION SUPPLEMENTARY BUDGET, PRIORITIZES K14.7 BILLION FOR MAIZE FARMERS

stories.title: 121st on fundamental rights, 109th on corruption: Chapter One says the 2026 Rule of Law Index shows authoritarian habits ‘becoming entrenched’
stories.excerpt: The Chapter One Foundation says the World Justice Project's 2026 index places Zambia among countries with a five-year decline in at least one safeguard against authoritarian rule, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer report. No government response to the index was reported, but in his maiden speech on Wednesday 21 October Monze East MP Jack Mwiimbu, until recently the Home Affairs minister, accused churches, civil society and the opposition of applauding those who abuse the President.

image.label: The 2026 Index
image.caption: The Chapter One Foundation's reading of the World Justice Project's 2026 Rule of Law Index, and a sharply different view from the Government benches.

body: The Chapter One Foundation said on Thursday 22 October that the World Justice Project's 2026 Rule of Law Index records a further slide in Zambia's adherence to the rule of law. Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer both carried the statement by its executive director, Josiah Kalala. The World Justice Project describes the 2026 edition of its index as covering 143 countries and jurisdictions.

According to both reports, Mr Kalala said Zambia is among the countries the index identifies as having suffered a sustained five-year decline in at least one of three safeguards against authoritarian rule: constraints on government powers, open government and fundamental rights. He cited rankings of 121st in the world, and 25th of 34 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, on fundamental rights; 111th on open government; 109th on absence of corruption; and 119th on regulatory enforcement. Neither report gives Zambia's overall score or its overall rank, nor the change from 2025.

body.text: authoritarian practices are no longer merely an emerging threat but are becoming entrenched.
body.attribution: Josiah Kalala, executive director of the Chapter One Foundation, in a statement reported by Zambia Monitor on Thursday 22 October

body: Mr Kalala pointed, according to Zambia Monitor, to documented deterioration in freedom of expression, assembly, association and civic participation, and to what he called an equally concerning decline in how effectively the judiciary limits government power. The Observer's account has him describing the findings as troubling because they suggested that "weaknesses in democratic safeguards were becoming entrenched rather than remaining isolated incidents of abuse". He urged the Government, Parliament, the Judiciary and other institutions to study the findings and pursue measurable reforms to strengthen institutional independence, protect freedoms and improve transparency.

body.text: The view from the Government benches

body: Neither outlet reported a Government response to the index itself. The same week, however, produced a forceful statement of the opposite case from a senior UPND MP. The Times of Zambia reports that Jack Mwiimbu, the Monze East MP and immediate past Minister of Home Affairs and Internal Security, used his maiden speech in Parliament on Wednesday 21 October to criticise church groups, civil-society organisations and the opposition for what he called their silence while critics of President Hakainde Hichilema wished him ill health and death. He said those groups were applauding people who abused the President, and that when law enforcement arrested lawbreakers it was the opposition, civil society and some churches who questioned the arrests.

body.text: Surely; is this the Zambia we want to be living in?
body.attribution: Jack Mwiimbu, Monze East MP, in his maiden speech to the National Assembly on Wednesday 21 October, as reported by the Times of Zambia

body: News Diggers reports that Mr Mwiimbu also said no responsible government could report security matters to citizens, even when asked how particular individuals had been arrested, and described as "impunity" the demand by a consortium of local and regional civil-society organisations that the Zambian and Mozambican governments account for the cross-border apprehension of Emmanuel Jay Banda. State House had already answered that consortium on Tuesday 20 October, as Lusaka Brief reported on Wednesday. The Times says Mr Mwiimbu challenged opposition members seeking dialogue with the President to come "with clean hands", and that the President had been the first to call for national unity and dialogue. Neither the Times nor News Diggers carried a reply from the churches, the civil-society groups or the opposition.

stories.title: Same seven faces at State House: Hichilema re-appoints his advisers from Machila to Kayumba, while the Cabinet of his second term is still awaited
stories.excerpt: President Hakainde Hichilema has re-appointed all seven members of his presidential advisory team, State House said in a statement on Thursday 22 October reported by Zambia Monitor and News Diggers. The re-appointments, under Article 92(2)(e) and (f) of the Constitution, retain officials who have served since 2021. They come in a week in which, News Diggers reports, UPND Alliance chairperson Charles Milupi was answering social-media claims that he would be left out of the Cabinet.

image.label: The advisory team
image.caption: President Hichilema has kept the seven advisers who served him through his first term, State House said on Thursday 22 October.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema has kept his inner circle of advisers intact. In a statement issued in Lusaka on Thursday 22 October, State House Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka announced that the President had re-appointed the seven members of his presidential advisory team under Article 92(2)(e) and (f) of the Constitution, Zambia Monitor and News Diggers report.

The seven are Bradford Machila as Principal Private Secretary; Christopher Mundia as Special Assistant to the President for Legal Affairs; Joseph Lungu as Special Assistant for Policy Compliance; Dr Lawrence Mwananyanda as Special Assistant for Projects Implementation Monitoring and National Security; Levy Ngoma as Special Assistant for Political Affairs; Dr Pamela Nakamba as Special Assistant for Economic Affairs; and Jito Kayumba as Special Assistant for Finance and Investments.

Zambia Monitor quotes Mr Hamasaka as saying the advisers "would continue serving in their respective roles", and reports that the President congratulated them and wished them well in their continued service. News Diggers describes the move as retaining officials who have served in the administration since 2021. Neither report says why fresh instruments of appointment were needed now, or for what term.

The announcement is notable as much for what it is not. It concerns the President's personal staff, not the ministers who will run the Government in his second term, and the composition of that Cabinet remains the subject of speculation. News Diggers reported on Wednesday 21 October that Charles Milupi, the UPND Alliance chairperson, had responded to social-media posts claiming he would be excluded from the Cabinet by saying he had no intention of retiring and that it was "up to President Hakainde Hichilema to appoint whoever he deems fit". He said he would accept an offer to serve in his previous ministry or any other, and remarked that competition for ministerial positions was strong and that some people were producing "fake" stories to remove those they saw as rivals.

Readers looking for the Government's own timetable will not find one in Thursday's statement: it names the advisers, confirms their roles and says nothing about the Cabinet. The advisers named are, according to News Diggers, officials who have served in the administration since 2021, so the practical effect is continuity at the top of the President's office while the ministerial line-up is settled.

stories.title: Second chair at the COMESA table: Hichilema becomes vice-chairperson as Mnangagwa takes over from Ruto in Harare and the bloc targets 15 per cent intra-regional trade
stories.excerpt: At the 25th COMESA Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare on Thursday 22 October, Zimbabwe's Emmerson Mnangagwa took the chair from Kenya's William Ruto and President Hakainde Hichilema was named vice-chairperson of the bloc's bureau, Lusaka Times, Kenya's Eastleigh Voice and Rwanda's KT Press report. The summit launched a 2026–2030 strategic plan that aims to lift trade among the 21 member states to 15 per cent of their total trade.

image.label: COMESA, Harare
image.caption: President Hichilema became vice-chairperson of COMESA at the bloc's 25th summit in Harare on Thursday 22 October.

body: President Hakainde Hichilema left Harare on Thursday 22 October with a new regional title. At the 25th Summit of COMESA Heads of State and Government, held at Zimbabwe's new Parliament building at Mt Hampden, Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa took over the chairmanship of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa from Kenya's William Ruto, and Mr Hichilema was named vice-chairperson of the COMESA bureau, Lusaka Times reports. Rwanda's KT Press, whose prime minister Justin Nsengiyumva represented President Paul Kagame, reports that Mr Mnangagwa congratulated Mr Hichilema on the appointment, and Kenya's Eastleigh Voice adds that Mr Ruto stays on the bureau as rapporteur.

Lusaka Times notes that Mr Ruto had held the chair since 2025; the Eastleigh Voice reports that Mr Mnangagwa's term runs for 2026–2027. The summit's theme was "One Market, One Future: Advancing Inclusive Industrialisation, Investment and Regional Integration in COMESA". Lusaka Times reported that the President was expected to hold bilateral talks on the sidelines, but published no outcomes from them.

The main business, according to the Eastleigh Voice and KT Press, was the launch of the COMESA Medium-Term Strategic Plan for 2026–2030 alongside the bloc's 2025 annual report. The plan sets a target of raising intra-COMESA trade to 15 per cent of the member states' total trade by 2030, and covers trade, industrialisation, infrastructure, digital transformation and value chains in agriculture, manufacturing and critical minerals.

In his handover remarks, as reported by the Eastleigh Voice, Mr Ruto said the bloc of 21 states, nearly 700 million people and a combined output above US$1 trillion still traded far more with the rest of the world than with itself. He set out five tasks for members: fully implement the COMESA Free Trade Area; adopt the COMESA business visa or ratify the protocol on free movement of persons; connect national payment systems to regional platforms; resolve reported trade barriers; and pay contributions to the bloc in full and on time.

body.text: Integration is only a success when it benefits the ordinary citizen.
body.attribution: Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe and incoming COMESA chairperson, at the summit in Harare on Thursday 22 October, as reported by KT Press

body: KT Press reports that Mr Mnangagwa called for better transport links, long-term financing for roads and railways, local processing of natural resources and climate-resilient agriculture, and that a final communiqué was expected after the meeting. Thursday's reports do not say when Mr Hichilema returns to Lusaka.

stories.title: Cranes that run on road and rail: Japan signs a 999 million yen grant for Zambia Railways maintenance equipment, with the two sides quoting the dollar figure differently
stories.excerpt: Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane and Japan's ambassador Mikami Akiteru exchanged notes in Lusaka on Thursday 22 October for a grant to buy Japanese-made railway maintenance equipment, including crane-equipped motor cars and road-rail crane trucks, Lusaka Times and Zambia Monitor report. The ambassador put the grant at 999 million yen, about US$6.3 million; the Ministry of Finance's announcement gave US$6.17 million.

image.label: Tokyo and the track
image.caption: Japan's grant will buy maintenance equipment for Zambia Railways under the Economic and Social Development Programme.

body: Zambia and Japan signed a grant agreement on Thursday 22 October to equip Zambia Railways with maintenance machinery made in Japan. Lusaka Times reports that Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane and Japan's ambassador, Mikami Akiteru, carried out an exchange of notes and signed the agreement at the ministry's offices in Lusaka under Japan's Economic and Social Development Programme. Zambia Monitor describes it as part of Japan's 2026 grant aid, and says the Secretary to the Treasury and the Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Transport and Logistics attended.

The two reports differ on the headline number. Lusaka Times gives US$6.3 million. Zambia Monitor reports that the Ministry of Finance announced a grant of US$6.17 million, while noting that the ambassador described it at the ceremony as roughly US$6.3 million, or 999 million yen, and that the gap was not explained. The yen figure is the one stated by the donor.

Both outlets report that the grant will pay for railway maintenance equipment, including crane-equipped motor cars and road-rail crane trucks that can travel on both roads and tracks. Lusaka Times says the purpose is to rehabilitate track and systems for Zambia Railways, cut transport costs and improve capacity to move minerals and agricultural produce to regional and international markets. Zambia Monitor quotes Mr Akiteru as saying the project would also support the use of transport corridors such as the Nacala Corridor.

body.text: Railways are vital infrastructure for economic and social development.
body.attribution: Mikami Akiteru, Ambassador of Japan to Zambia, at the signing ceremony in Lusaka on Thursday 22 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: Dr Musokotwane tied the grant to the Government's export-led growth plans. Lusaka Times quotes him as saying it "fits very neatly into our Grow Zambia Agenda of export-led growth", and that "to export, you need reliable transport and it must also be cheap". Zambia Monitor reports that he described the railway subsector as central to Zambia's ambition to become a regional transport and logistics hub, and quotes him thanking the Government and people of Japan on behalf of Zambia.

Mr Akiteru, according to Lusaka Times, said Zambia "is strategically located at the crossroads of major transport corridors in Southern Africa", and, according to Zambia Monitor, that Japanese rail systems were internationally recognised for safety, punctuality and efficiency and that the project would help Zambia move its natural resources more efficiently, attract investment and create jobs. Neither report gives a delivery date for the equipment or says which sections of the network it will serve first.

sources.title: Zambia, Japan Sign US$6.3 Million Grant Agreement For Railway Maintenance
Zambia secures $6.17 million Japanese grant for railway maintenance

stories.title: From the pit to the vault: ZCCM-IH tells London it will buy small-scale miners’ gold for the Bank of Zambia, citing a US$1.8 billion gap in the export data
stories.excerpt: ZCCM Investments Holdings chairperson Phesto Musonda told the Financial Times Africa Summit that the company's subsidiary Kyalo Goldfields will buy gold from licensed small-scale miners, pay them in kwacha and supply the metal to the Bank of Zambia, Zambia Monitor reports. He cited UAE records of nearly US$1.8 billion in gold imports from Zambia in 2023 against formal Zambian output of about 127,000 ounces last year — a discrepancy Africa Briefing traced in September to World Bank trade data.

image.label: Pit to vault
image.caption: ZCCM-IH says it will formalise the small-scale gold trade by buying metal for the Bank of Zambia's reserves.

body: The state mining investment company has taken its plan to formalise Zambia's gold trade to investors in London. Zambia Monitor reports that Phesto Musonda, board chairperson of ZCCM Investments Holdings Plc, told a panel on gold, sovereignty and stability at the Financial Times Africa Summit that the Government has mandated ZCCM-IH to lead the formalisation effort, and that its subsidiary Kyalo Goldfields will buy gold from licensed small-scale miners, pay them in kwacha and supply the metal to the Bank of Zambia to build national reserves. The remarks were released in a company statement on Thursday 22 October.

body.text: We are building a traceable chain, from the pit to the vault.
body.attribution: Phesto Musonda, board chairperson of ZCCM Investments Holdings, at the Financial Times Africa Summit in London, as reported by Zambia Monitor on Thursday 22 October

body: Mr Musonda's case rests on a gap in the numbers. According to Zambia Monitor he said the United Arab Emirates recorded nearly US$1.8 billion of gold imports from Zambia in 2023, while Zambia's formal gold output "last year" was about 127,000 ounces. He said lifting formal output to several hundred thousand ounces a year was achievable and that a traceable supply chain would improve confidence among international buyers and keep more of the metal's value in the country.

body.text: Where the US$1.8 billion figure comes from

body: Africa Briefing examined the same discrepancy in September. Citing the World Bank's World Integrated Trade Solution database for 2023, it reported that the UAE recorded imports of about 29.1 tonnes of non-monetary unwrought gold from Zambia worth about US$1.788 billion, while Zambia reported exports of the same product to the UAE of just US$61,800; Hong Kong recorded a further 2.03 tonnes worth US$107.6 million. Bank of Zambia figures cited in the same article put total declared gold export earnings at US$127.5 million in 2023, US$261.6 million in 2024 and US$345.6 million in 2025. Africa Briefing cautioned that mirror-trade gaps can arise from differences in valuation, timing and transit routes and do not by themselves prove smuggling, and it quoted ZCCM-IH chief executive Kakenenwa Muyangwa telling Bloomberg that formalisation could unlock more than US$1.8 billion.

The mandate is not new: Africa Briefing reports that the Government handed ZCCM-IH the lead on formalising, developing and transforming the gold sector in August 2025, and that Kyalo Goldfields was incorporated in May 2026 with partners to advance the Kikonge gold project in Mufumbwe District, North-Western Province. Ghana's Gold Board, whose artisanal and small-scale exports rose to about 103 tonnes in 2025, is the reference point in that report, which notes that Ghana's President John Mahama cited its results in an address to Zambia's Parliament.

What neither report yet contains is the operating detail: the prices Kyalo will pay, the volumes it expects, when buying starts, how many licensed small-scale miners are in the scheme, or any statement from the Bank of Zambia itself on taking the metal into reserves. Mr Musonda told the London audience, according to Zambia Monitor, that ZCCM-IH wanted to be the state's partner of choice for responsible mining and energy investment under what he called the Grow Zambia Agenda.

sources.title: Zambia's $1.8 billion gold export gap exposed as ZCCM-IH moves to formalise trade
Zambia eyes $1.8bn gold formalisation push

stories.title: ‘I was involved in bribing voters’: a former local-court magistrate turns petitioner’s witness in the Mwandi case, but says he has no evidence Iris Kaingu told him to do it
stories.excerpt: In the High Court sitting in Mongu, witnesses called by losing UPND candidate Sibeso Sefulo in her petition against independent Mwandi MP Iris Kaingu have admitted taking part in or receiving money during the August campaign, the Zambian Observer and News Diggers report. The former magistrate among them said he still supports Ms Kaingu and had no evidence she instructed any bribery; the judge warned the petitioner herself against interfering with a witness.

image.label: The Mwandi petition
image.caption: Witnesses in the petition against Mwandi MP Iris Kaingu admitted in court to giving or receiving money during the August campaign.

body: The petition to unseat Mwandi's independent MP, Iris Kaingu, produced a run of awkward admissions this week — not from the respondent's camp but from witnesses called by the petitioner. The Zambian Observer and News Diggers report that the High Court, sitting in Mongu before Judge Willie Sinyangwe, heard from a 41-year-old former Mwandi local-court magistrate who told the court he had been involved in bribing voters during the August parliamentary election. Under cross-examination by Ms Kaingu's lawyer, Isaac Simbeye, he answered "yes" when asked whether he had engaged in corrupt practices and bribery while working with her campaign, News Diggers reports.

The petitioner is Sibeso Sefulo, the UPND candidate who lost the seat. She is asking the court to nullify Ms Kaingu's election for alleged electoral bribery and corrupt practices. Ms Kaingu, who is represented by a team including Likando Kalaluka, has not been found to have done anything wrong; the court was still hearing and cross-examining the petitioner's witnesses, and the Observer notes that her position has so far been put only through her lawyers' cross-examination.

According to the Observer, the former magistrate said he still supported Ms Kaingu and had voted for her even though he wanted her election nullified, that he had no evidence she instructed him to bribe anyone, and that her father, Michael Kaingu, had invited him to join the campaign and given him K1,000 — a gift in which he said he saw nothing wrong. He denied that he was testifying in the hope of having an assault case against him withdrawn, and said he could not recall the circumstances of his dismissal from the Judiciary but denied it was linked to corruption.

Other petitioner's witnesses, the Observer reports, included a UPND youth chairperson who said he voted for Ms Kaingu because she had given K1,000 towards a wedding, a UPND ward chairlady who said she had received and spent money handed out at a polling station on 13 August and had not reported it to police, and a church choir secretary who said she had received K1,000 from the former magistrate — which he had denied giving — and had voted for Ms Kaingu because of the donation, while rejecting counsel's suggestion that the word for it was "corruption". Lusaka Brief is not naming these witnesses: none has been charged with any offence.

The court's patience was tested. Both outlets report that Judge Sinyangwe warned Ms Sefulo against interfering with a witness and threatened to have her removed from the courtroom, after Mr Kalaluka objected that the public gallery was disturbing a witness. A dispute over one witness's answer about an alleged K500 payment was blamed by the petitioner's lawyer on difficulties of interpretation from Lozi, and by Mr Kalaluka on the witness changing her answer after noise from the gallery.

body.confirmed: That the petition by Sibeso Sefulo against Iris Kaingu is being heard by Judge Willie Sinyangwe in Mongu; that a former Mwandi local-court magistrate told the court he had been involved in bribing voters; that several petitioner's witnesses admitted receiving money; and that the judge warned the petitioner over interference with a witness — all reported by the Zambian Observer and News Diggers.
body.unverified: Whether any of the money described was given at Ms Kaingu's direction, which the former magistrate said he could not show; the Electoral Commission's position, which neither report describes; when the respondent's case opens; and when judgment can be expected. Nothing in this week's evidence amounts to a finding against the MP.

sources.title: MWANDI MP ELECTION PETITION: WITNESSES ADMIT RECEIVING MONEY, VOTING FOR KAINGU
Ex-Magistrate admits bribing voters in Mwandi

stories.title: Thirty grammes and a famous name: the DEC says it has arrested rapper Chanda of ‘Chanda na Kay’ for alleged cannabis trafficking; he has not yet answered the claim
stories.excerpt: The Drug Enforcement Commission said in a statement on Thursday 22 October that it had arrested Edward Chanda, 28, the Lusaka rapper known as Chanda of the duo Chanda na Kay, for allegedly trafficking 30.3 grammes of dry loose cannabis, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer report. The arrest was announced alongside operations in Lusaka, Muchinga and Southern provinces. Mr Chanda has not yet appeared in court on the new allegation and his response has not been reported.

image.label: The DEC statement
image.caption: The Drug Enforcement Commission announced the arrest of rapper Edward Chanda on Thursday 22 October as part of operations in three provinces.

body: A popular Zambian musician is in the hands of the Drug Enforcement Commission. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer report that the DEC announced on Thursday 22 October the arrest of Edward Chanda, 28, a resident of Meanwood in Lusaka who performs as Chanda and is one half of the duo Chanda na Kay, for the alleged trafficking of 30.3 grammes of dry loose cannabis.

The announcement came from the commission's public relations officer, Allan Tamba. The Observer, carrying a Sun FM report, quotes his statement as describing the suspect as "the 28-year-old musician, popularly known by his stage name CHANDA, is a resident of Meanwood in Lusaka". Both outlets report that Mr Tamba placed the arrest within what he called intelligence-led operations targeting drug trafficking networks in Lusaka, Muchinga and Southern provinces, which he said had produced several arrests and significant seizures. News Diggers reports that the same statement announced the arrest of a 22-year-old man described by the commission as a suspected trafficking kingpin known as "Ghost".

The commission's statement describes the allegation as trafficking. What the statement, as reported, does not say is when Mr Chanda will appear in court, whether he has been released on bond, or what he says about the allegation. Neither outlet reported a response from him or his management by Thursday evening. He is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

The arrest is not his first encounter with the authorities this year. News Diggers reports that Mr Chanda was arrested earlier in 2026 on charges of child trafficking and child grooming, and that he pleaded not guilty to those charges. That case is separate from the DEC's allegation and its status was not reported on Thursday.

body.confirmed: That the DEC announced on Thursday 22 October the arrest of Edward Chanda, 28, for alleged trafficking of 30.3 grammes of cannabis, as part of operations in Lusaka, Muchinga and Southern provinces — reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer from the commission's statement.
body.unverified: Any account of events from Mr Chanda himself; the date of any court appearance; whether he is on bond; and the current status of the earlier, separate case in which he pleaded not guilty.

sources.title: DEC nabs Chanda of 'Chanda na Kay' for drug trafficking
DEC Arrests Popular Zambian Musician Chanda for allegedly trafficking 30.3 grammes of dry cannabis

stories.title: One goal to protect in Durban: Red Arrows meet Kaizer Chiefs at Moses Mabhida at 15:00 today with a Confederation Cup group place at stake
stories.excerpt: Red Arrows carry Alassane Diarra's 76th-minute winner from Ndola into the second leg of their CAF Confederation Cup second preliminary round tie against Kaizer Chiefs at Moses Mabhida Stadium in Durban on Friday 23 October, kick-off 15:00 Central African Time, ZamFoot reports. Coach Chisi Mbewe says his side is braced for an all-out Chiefs performance; assistant Kalililo Kakonje says the players know what is at stake.

image.label: Arrows in Durban
image.caption: Red Arrows defend a 1–0 first-leg lead against Kaizer Chiefs in Durban on Friday 23 October.

body: Red Arrows have 90 minutes in Durban to turn a one-goal lead into a place in the group stage of the CAF Confederation Cup. The second leg of their second preliminary round tie against Kaizer Chiefs kicks off at Moses Mabhida Stadium at 15:00 Central African Time on Friday 23 October, ZamFoot reports. The Zambian Premier League side won the first leg 1–0 at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola, where Alassane Diarra scored the only goal in the 76th minute, according to Africa Soccer.

That first leg, played on Saturday 17 October, was closer than the scoreline. Africa Soccer reports that Arrows created several chances and missed others before Diarra's late strike, and quotes coach Chisi Mbewe telling ZamFoot afterwards that his players had shown great commitment despite the missed opportunities, and that the team needed to stay compact in South Africa and deny Chiefs the space to control the game.

body.text: What the two camps are saying

body: News Diggers reports that the squad flew to South Africa on Wednesday 21 October and that Mr Mbewe said his side was bracing for an all-out approach from Chiefs, had tightened its preparations accordingly, and had found the travelling squad difficult to select. His first assistant, Kalililo Kakonje, told ZamFoot that the players had prepared adequately and understood that a disciplined performance was needed to protect the lead.

body.text: We are ready for the game. We know what is at stake.
body.attribution: Kalililo Kakonje, Red Arrows first assistant coach, speaking to ZamFoot before the team's departure, as reported on Thursday 22 October

body: Kaizer Chiefs, who play in South Africa's Betway Premiership, have framed the return leg as a rescue mission. The club's own website carried pieces on Thursday 22 October headed "Amakhosi determined to turn Red Arrows tie around" and "Chiefs boosted by key returns ahead of CAF clash", and its preview of the first leg had already looked ahead to "next week's decisive second-leg clash in Durban".

The prize is a place in the Confederation Cup group stage, which would, ZamFoot says, make Arrows one of five Zambian representatives to reach that phase. Neither ZamFoot nor News Diggers reports the travelling squad or any injury news, and no kick-off time other than 15:00 Central African Time has been published.

stories.title: Thirteen schoolboys in Baku: Zambia’s Under-15s open the first FIFA U-15 World Cup on Saturday in a group with Uruguay, Tanzania, Comoros, Moldova and Montserrat
stories.excerpt: Brian Kunsanama's 13-player squad, drawn largely from secondary and primary schools, left Lusaka on Tuesday 20 October for the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, Azerbaijan, which starts on Saturday 24 October, ZamFoot reports. Africa Top Sports places Zambia in Group X with Uruguay, Tanzania, Comoros, Moldova and Montserrat in a tournament played in an eight-a-side format.

image.label: Under-15s in Baku
image.caption: Zambia's Under-15 boys play in the first FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, Azerbaijan, from Saturday 24 October.

body: Zambia's youngest national team on the road this week is also its newest. The Under-15 boys flew out of Kenneth Kaunda International Airport at 21:00 on Tuesday 20 October for the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, Azerbaijan, ZamFoot reports. The tournament opens on Saturday 24 October; ZamFoot gives the closing date as 31 October and Africa Top Sports as 30 October.

Head coach Brian Kunsanama has named a squad of 13, and the clubs listed against the names tell their own story about where Zambian football finds its 14- and 15-year-olds. According to ZamFoot the goalkeepers are Abraham Bwalya of Munali Boys Secondary School and Patrick Mudenda of Billy Pro Sports; the defenders Moses Mushota of Barotse Crocs, Maybin Phiri of Mockved and Thomson Mwashilindji of Young Crocs; the midfielders Moses Munkombwe, also of Munali Boys, Adrian Kasanda of Mpelembe Secondary School, Jabulani Nyirenda of Arakan Secondary School, Peter Mwansa of Mahatma Gandhi and Chrispin Katoba of Kine Primary School; and the strikers Benson Bwalya of Tunduya Primary School, Samuel Musonda of Sporting Lusaka and Maksen Msimuko of Young Crocs.

body.text: A different kind of World Cup

body: Africa Top Sports reports that FIFA has given the new competition an eight-a-side format intended to develop young players through small-sided games, and that Zambia have been drawn in Group X alongside Comoros, Moldova, Montserrat, Tanzania and Uruguay. Neither report gives Zambia's individual fixture dates or explains how the entrants were selected. The squad held a week-long training camp in Lusaka and had been together for at least 14 days before departure, with some players having featured in a schools' tournament in Zimbabwe.

body.text: The team is ready, the boys have been pushing.
body.attribution: Brian Kunsanama, Zambia Under-15 head coach, before the team's departure, as reported by Africa Top Sports on Wednesday 21 October

body: Mr Kunsanama was careful to describe the trip as development first. Africa Top Sports quotes him as saying it was "obviously" a developmental tournament in which he wanted to expose as many players as possible, while adding: "But we have to win because winning should be part of development." Neither report says how the squad will be followed from home or whether the matches will be broadcast in Zambia.

analysis.title: The maize bill was a choice as much as a surprise; the borrowing is the part to watch
analysis.body: The second supplementary budget is easy to read as a bumper-harvest accident: farmers grew far more than the Food Reserve Agency planned to buy, and the Treasury must now find the money. But both Thursday's reports make clear that the overshoot — 2.7 million tonnes against a 500,000-tonne target — followed a deliberate decision to stock reserves ahead of a lean 2027 season. The case for that decision is straightforward: a full silo is cheaper than emergency imports in a drought year, and paying farmers keeps rural cash flowing. The case against is in the financing table. K18 billion of the K19.9 billion is to come from extra domestic borrowing, which competes with private borrowers for the same kwacha and arrives while the Government is also asking lenders to back a 'growth, growth, growth' agenda. What is still unknown is when farmers will actually be paid, what the revised Annual Borrowing Plan will cost, and what the roughly K1.5 billion not itemised in either report is for. Watch the Expanded Planning and Budgeting Committee's report, and whether any MP presses on the first two questions.

analysis.title: Two readings of the same country: the Rule of Law Index and the view from Monze East
analysis.body: Thursday offered Zambians two sharply different accounts of their democracy within 24 hours. The Chapter One Foundation read the World Justice Project's 2026 index as evidence that authoritarian practices are 'becoming entrenched', citing rankings in the low 100s on fundamental rights, open government and corruption. The day before, Jack Mwiimbu, the immediate past Home Affairs minister, told Parliament that the real failure lay with churches, civil society and the opposition for questioning lawful arrests and staying silent when the President was abused. Neither side was answering the other directly, and that is the gap to notice. The index measures perceptions and expert assessments of institutions over time; Mr Mwiimbu's speech addressed the conduct of particular critics. Both can be true at once: a government can act lawfully in individual cases while the institutions around it are judged to be weakening. What is not yet known is Zambia's overall score and how far it moved, which neither report gave, and whether the Government will respond to the index on its merits. Watch for a formal reaction from the Ministry of Justice and for how Parliament's new opposition leadership handles the question.

analysis.title: The gold gap is real in the data; whether Kyalo can close it depends on the price it pays
analysis.body: ZCCM-IH's London pitch rests on a striking contrast: foreign customs records showing well over a billion dollars of Zambian gold arriving in Dubai in a single year, against declared national output of around 127,000 ounces. The mirror-trade data that Africa Briefing traced in September support the scale of the discrepancy, but the same report's caution deserves equal weight — valuation, timing and transit routes can inflate such gaps, and not every undeclared ounce is a smuggled one. The formalisation model is borrowed from Ghana's Gold Board, whose artisanal exports have risen sharply, and the logic is sound: give licensed small-scale miners a legal buyer who pays promptly in kwacha, and route the metal to the central bank. The unanswered question is price. Africa Briefing's own test is the right one: competitive prices, reliable payments, accessible buying centres and licensing rules that do not push small operators back into informal networks. Still unknown are Kyalo's buying prices, its volumes and start date, how many licensed miners it can reach, and the Bank of Zambia's own view on taking the metal into reserves. Those are the details to watch for before judging whether the pit-to-vault chain is a policy or a slogan.
